brief.head: Cruise control, coded
brief.text: Cruise control and automatic transmission once needed very clever mechanical engineers, Ajay Shah said. With cheap CPUs, each becomes a trivial bit of code. {087-C04}

brief.head: More is not faster
brief.text: Doubling transistors did not double CPU speed, Ajay Shah said. Clever tricks wrung out about tenfold, then maxed out; the answer was the GPU’s thousand small processors. {087-C06}

brief.head: Musk’s phone and mine
brief.text: Technology is a great equaliser, Amit Varma argued: GPS went from the military to luxury cars to everyone, and his phone is not very different from Elon Musk’s. {087-C15}

brief.head: Practice, with purpose
brief.text: Volume alone is not enough, Amit Varma said. A boy at the cricket nets should work on footwork, elbow, balance and a still head, one quality at a time. {087-C09}

brief.head: Pillows from space
brief.text: Lift a constraint and humans fill the space, Amit Varma said. GPS now gets his pizza to him; memory-foam pillows built for spacecraft now sit in ordinary homes. {087-C17}

thought.text: Perfection is the enemy of production.
thought.who: Amit Varma, urging creators to have a bias for action

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on technological progress
lead.head: Moore makes more, for less
body: The episode began with an exam. Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah for the sum of the squares of the first four primes. Shah added aloud, landed on 87, and the episode had its number. {087-J01}

Then Shah had to pitch his topic like a job applicant. His subject was Moore’s Laws, plural, and what followed was a conversation on why the modern world keeps getting better and cheaper, and what that says about people.
## A social fact
Moore’s Law, in Shah’s bumper-sticker version, says the number of transistors on a chip doubles every 18 months or so. Gordon Moore saw the pattern in a 1965 paper that rested on seven data points.
The Intel 4004, the first CPU on a single chip, did the whole job with about 2,300 transistors. Our phones now squander billions.
Nothing in nature guarantees the doubling, Shah stressed. “This is not a physics law,” he said. “It’s not a physical fact about the universe. It’s a social fact. It’s an economic fact.” {087-C02}

Draw it with time on one axis and a log scale on the other, and the doubling becomes a straight line. Shah’s phrase for it, which recurred through the episode, was “straight lines on a semi-log graph”.
## The plural
Billions of transistors would be a curiosity, Shah said, if each chip cost a million dollars. The more important version of the law, perhaps five times more, puts price on the y-axis.

The same straight lines turn up in solar panels, bandwidth, lithium-ion batteries, DNA sequencing and the cost of sending a kilo into orbit. “As an economist, I just want to say that’s the whole enchilada,” he said. “You’ve got to get the prices down.” {087-C03}

Then came two rival laws. Wright’s Law, from 1936, puts lifetime output on the x-axis: roughly a 20 per cent productivity gain for every doubling. Goddard’s Law credits annual scale. A study of 62 industries, Shah said, found Wright’s the best predictor.
“Not time. Volume,” he said. “You put in volume and you will get improvements.”
Varma drew a lesson for creators: do, do, do. Shah added the caveat that the gains are a frontier, earned only by firms that work at them.
## A shared religion

The law also solves a puzzle, Shah argued. A chip needs ASML’s machines in Holland, American design software, thousands of engineers in Bangalore and hundreds of other firms. No government coordinates them.

Instead the industry “signed up for the religion” of the 18-month doubling, so each firm dared to invest ahead of the rest. “It became a coordination mechanism by hundreds of firms,” he said. {087-C12}
Varma’s gloss was that the articulation of the law matters as much as the law: a shared dream makes action look coordinated when it is not.
For Varma the deeper story was human: people, he said, are brains, not stomachs.
Near the end, Shah made a confession. He had underrated digital cameras and lithium-ion batteries, even as an enthusiast. “Humans are not good at exponential thinking,” he said. {087-C14}
Varma’s advice to young entrepreneurs followed from it: “Make for the future. Don’t make for today.”

second.label: The Ehrlich–Simon bet
second.head: Simon says: prices fall
second.deck: Amit Varma on a 1980 wager between gloom and ingenuity
body: Paul Ehrlich made Malthusian predictions, Amit Varma said. In the early seventies he said Britain would be extinct by 2000, and that half of India would starve by the end of the decade. {#ehrlich}

Julian Simon, whom Varma called a great economist, found such claims ridiculous. In 1980 the two bet on the prices of five materials, chosen by Ehrlich, over ten years. If population rose and resources did not, Malthusian logic said prices would rise. {087-S08}
All five fell, and Simon won. “We kept innovating, we kept doing funky things,” Varma said. For him the bet is evidence that people are brains, not stomachs. {087-C16}

quote.text: Julian Simon was like, No, hold on, man. We are innovative, we are creative, that is a core of progress.

second.caption: the Ehrlich–Simon wager

third.head: Make ten pots, not one
body: Amit Varma cited an experiment whose details, he admitted, he had forgotten. One group had a month to make a single perfect pot. {#pots} The other had to make ten pots a day, and their best would be judged.
The perfectionists’ pot came out mediocre. The volume group quickly passed that standard and went on to make really good pots.

For Varma, this is Wright’s Law for the creator economy. Many creators get stuck chasing the perfect blog, the perfect YouTube show, the perfect episode. “The key to excellence is not to spend forever over trying to make something perfect, but doing, doing, doing, doing, doing,” he said. {087-C08}
Do that, and “your baseline level gets so high that excellence automatically emerges”. {087-S04}
third.caption: ten pots a day

p2.title: The laws of progress
p2.deck: Moore’s Law, its plural, two rival laws and the faith that keeps an industry in step

sections.label: The first law
sections.head: Seven dots and a straight line
sections.caption: the law that isn’t physics
body: The transistor, Ajay Shah said, is a thing with three prongs, first made in 1947 and assembled by hand at Bell Labs. Then came the pressure to do more, and the most important customers were in space research.

NASA was desperate to put small, compact equipment on satellites. {#nasa} Its funding, Shah said, literally created the industry: integrated circuits, then very large scale integration, then the Intel 4004.
That chip had something like 2,300 transistors, a figure Shah offered to “all ye callow gentle readers” who squander billions on their phones. {087-J05}
## Fetch, add, branch
At heart, he explained, a CPU is a Turing machine. It needs to fetch a memory cell into a register, to add, and to branch on an if. “Everything else is toppings.” {087-C01}

Gordon Moore saw the pattern in seven components and hypothesised about what was going on. The doubling, roughly every 18 months, has run for decades since. Plotted on a semi-log graph, it gives a tenfold rise every few years.

Amit Varma reached for the old parable of the king and the chessboard: one grain of rice on the first square, doubled on each square after. Shah worked out the total in kilograms against the mass of the earth and declared it “well beyond the resources of any king”.
~ Varma was unmoved. “Doesn’t matter,” he said. “It’s a lot of grain.” {087-J04}

quote.text: It’s an economic law that we are able to pile on the innovations and the capital intensity

sections.label: What it did
sections.head: When engineering became code
sections.caption: cheap chips everywhere
body: Computation became ubiquitous and cheap, Ajay Shah said. A mind-blowing CPU can cost a dollar or ten cents, cheap enough to waste. You can put one in a toaster.

That turned old triumphs of mechanical engineering into trivial software. Cruise control, which holds Shah’s car at the 100 kph limit on the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, once needed very clever people. Now it is a few lines: push the speed up below 99, down above 101. {087-C04}
## Leaps and grinding

Not all progress is like this. Lighting went from candles to gas lamps, tungsten, fluorescent tubes and LEDs, from about 9 per cent efficiency to 90. But it came in jumps between stagnations, and that journey, Shah said, is now over. {087-C05}
Amit Varma saw two kinds of learning in this: steady accumulation, or a leap, then refinement, then another leap.

More transistors did not even make CPUs faster. Built on the single-threaded PDP-11 model, they mostly sat waiting for memory. Tricks such as computing both sides of an if squeezed out about tenfold, then maxed out. The GPU, a thousand small processors on one chip, was the way through.

~ Varma, who calls himself the best driver in Bombay thanks partly to automatic transmission, asked whether manual versus automatic was a question “akin to the Oxford comma and the semicolon”. {087-J06}

quote.text: What we are describing as Moore’s Law is just this madness of grinding away year after year, the damn thing gets better.

sections.label: Moore’s Laws
sections.head: Cheaper by the doubling
sections.caption: price on the y-axis
body: Technology is a great equaliser, Amit Varma argued, against those on the left who say it widens inequality. It starts with governments or the rich and reaches everyone, and falling prices are what carry it there. {087-C15}

Ajay Shah took up the point, and explained the plural in the episode’s title. Put price, or performance per price, on the y-axis and the straight lines appear again. Solar panels began as exotic kit on satellites. {#solar} Their rival there, the plutonium battery, never got the same price gains.
## A university on one line

When Shah was a PhD student in America, the whole University of Southern California ran on a T1 line of about 1.5 megabits a second, “the height of cool”. Today a home connection gives something like 300, for less. {087-S02}
Launch costs fell in the sixties and seventies, then stagnated for a long time. Now private firms are innovating again, and people predict $10 a kilo to near-earth orbit. {#tenkg}

Varma remembered dial-up: the sound of the modem, and “half a picture of Samantha Fox” before the line dropped. Shah went one better: he could hear the modem negotiate and tell which protocol it got through. {087-J07}
~ Today, Varma said, broadband is effectively free and effectively everywhere.

quote.text: The cell phone that I use is not very different from the cell phone Elon Musk uses.

sections.label: Two more laws
sections.head: Volume, not the calendar
sections.caption: Wright’s Law and the learning curve
body: Ajay Shah offered two rivals to Moore’s Law. Wright’s Law, from 1936, by a man who was not one of the Wright brothers, says productivity rises with lifetime volume, about 20 per cent for every doubling. Goddard’s Law credits scale in a single year. {087-C07}

Nagy and colleagues tested them across 62 industries and found Wright’s the best. So, Shah said, judge a person by lifetime output: a cobbler who has repaired 53,000 shoes is “standing on something great”. {#cobbler}
Amit Varma applied it to the show: by episode 174 they would be 20 per cent better. Shah agreed, but noted the learning rate had already slowed. {087-J08}
## Why firms stall

The gains are not preordained, Shah warned. Bad firms run consultant-chosen machines like helpless peasants and wait for the next upgrade. They churn their teams, so tacit knowledge walks out. And they are cut to the bone, with no slack for thinking or mistakes. {087-C11}
He cited a line from *Even Cowgirls Get the Blues*: the only people on routine flights are those who think they are on routine flights. {087-R09}
~ Varma added Anders Ericsson’s idea of deliberate practice: volume works only when you think about what you are doing.

quote.text: But when you lack the fat, thinking, for strategy, for innovation, for making mistakes. Then actually you don’t get on these journeys to quality.

sections.label: I, CPU
sections.head: No planner, no problem
sections.caption: an industry that coordinates itself
body: Amit Varma raised Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil*, on how a humble pencil needs millions of people to coordinate through prices. Ajay Shah upped the stakes: “I, Pencil does not hold a candle to I, CPU.” {#pencil}
A chip draws on ASML’s machines in Holland, three American firms’ design software, tens of thousands of engineers in Bangalore, and ARM, Apple, Intel and hundreds more. {#bangalore}

Classic Mahalanobis-style thinking, Shah said, holds that only a government could coerce all of them into step. Yet no government plays that role. The shared, near-religious belief in the 18-month doubling does. {087-C12}
## Ten years ahead

ASML saw a decade early that conventional lithography would max out and that chipmaking would need extreme ultraviolet light. Nobody knew how; the physics was severe; rival firms failed. ASML kept investing for years and got through. {087-S07}
The same faith now funds AI, Shah said, at outrageous cost. A Gemini API call costs about fifty paise, too much for most Indian apps. {#gemini} His challenge: dream of the day it costs 0.05 paise.
~ That, Shah said, is the glory of Moore’s Law: users are told to close their eyes and dream.

quote.text: So Moore’s Law has this very interesting idea that it’s a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy.

sections.label: The bigger picture
sections.head: From whale oil to the cloud
sections.caption: human ingenuity
body: For Amit Varma, the episode was finally “a humanity story”. Each time an energy source looked exhausted, he said, scarcity raised prices and set off innovation: wood gave way to coal, whale oil to fossil fuels, and nuclear and renewables now promise a way beyond. {087-C16}

Around 2000, big companies sank more than $100 billion into fibre-optic cable across America. After the dot-com bust, 90 per cent of it lay unused, and people called it a waste. On it came broadband, mobile telephony and cloud computing; today 80 to 90 per cent is in use. {087-S09}
## Missing the curve

Ajay Shah confessed his own failures of foresight. A hardcore analog photographer, shooting Kodachrome and Ektachrome on Nikons, he thought early digital gear hopelessly shabby. He was wrong about lithium-ion batteries too, despite many evenings dreaming about them with Ayush Patnaik. {087-S10}
His test for any firm: plot productivity against lifetime volume on a log scale. No straight line means something is wrong with the organisation and its culture. {087-C10}
~ Varma pointed to Netflix, which bet on streaming in 2007 before bandwidth and displays were ready. Today, he warned, “will be an artifact by the time twenty-four hours are over”. {087-C13}

quote.text: And I failed to see that you just have to give it ten, twenty years, and these gaps will be overcome.

side.boxText: Gordon Moore set out the law in a 1965 paper using just seven data points. “All you need is seven good data points to get a world changing observation,” Ajay Shah said. The law, he stressed, is economics, not physics. {087-C02}

contQuote.text: Humans are incredible at maximizing within their constraints. As you lift those constraints, as those boundaries expand, as capacity expands, humans will innovate and fill that space.

p3.title: Tales from the curve
p3.deck: A bankrupting hit, a generous hotel, a phone in Africa, a masterpiece by accident

stories.start: That was around the time the middle of two thousand the Nasdaq crash
stories.end: because we were successful in getting traffic and we were successful in user acquisition
stories.caption: the quiz that sank him
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s quiz game of 2000, and its traffic bill
stories.head: Second in India, first in debt
body: In the middle of 2000, the Nasdaq had crashed, the investors in Amit Varma’s first startup had backed out, and *Kaun Banega Crorepati* was just becoming a hit. Varma, a hardcore quizzer, wanted to make something immersive online.

He built Crow Master, a gamified quiz with a quizmaster called Babu Moshai, “quite cheesy”, he admitted. He paid quizzing friends for a bank of thousands of questions. It asked a question, replied to your answer, perhaps offered clues, then moved on. It lived on a site called Mindfever.com, alongside other interactive games.
There was even a way to make money: players could be billed through the telephone company, on their phone bills.
Every answer pinged the server, so the server had to be close to the players. Varma hosted on VSNL rather than abroad. VSNL charged by traffic: the more visitors, the more you paid.
The game went “madly viral”. For one month it was the number two site in India, somewhere between Rediff and Cricinfo. {#numbertwo}
Star’s digital arm in Bangalore offered to buy it, for a sum Varma half-remembers as fifty lakh or a crore. Then the arm shut down, a casualty of the Nasdaq crash.

“But that one month bankrupted us and took us hugely into debt because we were paying according to the traffic,” Varma said. {087-S03} The site shut after about three months, and he was left owing a lot of money.
~ None of it exists now, he said, “not even written about”.
stories.why: Where you sit on the cost curve decides whether success makes you or breaks you. In 2000, every visitor cost Varma money; today, he said, no one pays for traffic that way.
stories.postscript: The first of Varma’s two startups, and why it failed, came up in the previous episode.

stories.start: This story is about the hotel chain Ritt Scalten
stories.end: conference to this hotel and is held there every year from that time on
stories.caption: the Ritz-Carlton’s $2,000 rule
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a hotel that trusted its staff
stories.head: A ring, a laptop, a tank engine
body: Amit Varma had it from a Twitter thread by Ben Wolff. In 1983 Horst Schulze, leading the Ritz-Carlton, let every employee spend up to $2,000 of the hotel’s money on a guest without asking anyone. A regular guest, he reckoned, was worth $200,000 over a lifetime. {#ritz}
One employee flew from Atlanta to Hawaii to return a guest’s laptop. A child’s Thomas the Tank Engine, which Varma would not call a toy, came home with photographs of Thomas enjoying spa treatment.
A couple in Cancun lost their wedding ring on the beach the day before the wedding. An employee bought four metal detectors, and staff searched all night until they found it. {#metal}
~ A server overheard diners planning a conference at another hotel, and comped their $600 dinner. They moved the conference to the Ritz, where it was held every year after. {#comp}

quote.text: $2,000 was a very small amount of money to make people feel that this was their place.

stories.postscript: Varma’s own case: in 2008, flying back after his mother died, his family got a free upgrade to business class at the counter. {087-S06}

stories.start: Larry Summers uh tells this story of the most dramatic technical change
stories.end: to reach from some exotic technology in America to a river crossing in Africa
stories.caption: the phone in the car
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells a story from the economist Larry Summers
stories.head: This call is for you
body: Larry Summers, Ajay Shah said, tells a story of the most dramatic technical change of his life. Shah placed it around the 1992 United States elections, when Summers was an adviser to Michael Dukakis and there was a Democratic convention, he thought, in Chicago.
A car was sent to pick Summers up, and it had a phone in it. He had never seen a phone in a car. So he picked it up and called his wife: he was calling her from a car.
“A scant one and a half years later,” Shah said, Summers was crossing a river in Africa when somebody handed him a GSM phone and said: “This call is for you.” {087-S01}
~ That, said Shah, is how the stuff got democratised and went all over the world.
stories.why: When a technology rides a falling price curve, its spread is measured in months, not generations. That, for Ajay Shah, is why the price version of Moore’s Law matters: the exotic toy becomes everyday kit. {087-C03}

stories.start: for Astral Weeks what happened was that When he wrote this bunch of songs
stories.end: No, you fucker, I'm a jazz player, I'll do something different each time
stories.caption: an accidental masterpiece
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recommendation, and the story behind it
stories.head: Sacked band, saved album
body: Van Morrison took a couple of his own musicians to the studio to record *Astral Weeks*. The producer, who had his own ideas, quickly sacked them and brought in his own crew, including the bassist Richard Davis.
Morrison sang and played guitar while jazz musicians improvised around him. “It was a bunch of jazz guys improvising,” Amit Varma said. “And the result is an absolute masterpiece.” {087-S11}
Morrison was not happy at first, because it did not match the picture in his head. Over time he came to see it as a masterpiece.

~ Some thirty years later, if Varma remembered correctly, Morrison toured with Davis and wanted the parts played exactly as on the album. Davis, in Varma’s telling, refused colourfully: he was a jazz player and would do something different each time. {087-J10}
stories.why: The best work sometimes comes from losing control. Morrison’s plan did not survive the producer, and his album was the better for it; nor was he, in the moment, the best judge of what he had made.
stories.postscript: Varma pairs it with *Moondance*, Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the traditional way. {087-R02}

quiz.q: What sum did Ajay Shah compute to arrive at the episode’s number, 87?
quiz.a: The sum of the squares of the first four primes: 4, 9, 25 and 49.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah call Moore’s Law an economic law rather than a law of physics?
quiz.a: Nothing in nature guarantees the doubling; it holds because people keep piling on innovation and capital.

quiz.q: What does Wright’s Law put on the x-axis, and what gain does it predict?
quiz.a: Cumulative lifetime output; roughly a 20 per cent productivity gain for every doubling.

quiz.q: What three things, according to Ajay Shah, does a CPU need to be able to do?
quiz.a: Fetch a memory cell into a register, add, and branch on an if.

quiz.q: How much could any Ritz-Carlton employee spend on a guest without asking anyone, from 1983?
quiz.a: Up to $2,000, against a regular guest’s lifetime value of $200,000.

quiz.q: Which company in Holland bet a decade early on extreme ultraviolet lithography, and why?
quiz.a: ASML, which projected Moore’s Law ten years ahead and saw conventional lithography maxing out.
